paragraphs.text: Laser Cutting for Dummies

paragraphs.name: d727
paragraphs.text: Editor’s note: Hongyi interned with us in February and March in 2019. She’d just finished her A-levels, and will be starting her undergraduate studies later this year. Here’s her contribution to our blog:

paragraphs.name: bba0
paragraphs.text: I had my first experience laser-cutting some weeks ago. It was pretty sweet. Laser cutting can be quite daunting for a first-timer. Is this loud sound normal? Will the machine explode?

paragraphs.name: 0cbc
paragraphs.text: Here are some of the essential to-know’s for my fellow first-time laser cutters!

paragraphs.name: 3e21
paragraphs.text: Just Starting Out..

paragraphs.name: 87cf
paragraphs.text: Get the right equipment. Make sure you have a laser cutter. I used Full Spectrum Laser Cutter. To create a vector drawing (for cutting), I used Inkscape. It might be slightly different if you used different equipment and software but the gist and underlying principles in this article should remain the same.

paragraphs.name: eddf
paragraphs.text: Creating Your Drawing

paragraphs.name: 9ef2
paragraphs.text: I am an artist!

paragraphs.name: 6f21
paragraphs.text: I used Inkscape to create my drawings. I highly recommend going through the four Inkscape tutorials below if you have never used Inkscape before. These are the ones I found useful inducting me to this whole vector-drawing-verse. Don’t worry too much about the keyboard commands if you are not a fan. I seldom use them, and I did alright. I have outlined what’s important in each tutorial below.

paragraphs.name: 9c9f
paragraphs.text: Basics: Know how to zoom, move, rotate, scale, duplicate, align and group shapes. Also know how to fill and stroke a shape.

paragraphs.name: fb3d
paragraphs.text: “Advanced”: Pasting tricks, simplifying paths.

paragraphs.name: dd5c
paragraphs.text: Tracing Bitmaps: If you are lazy to make your own vector drawing, you can convert an existing image and work from there.

paragraphs.name: 598d
paragraphs.text: Editing Paths by Nodes: Since we are working with .svg vector drawings, knowing how to edit paths by nodes will give you that added precision and control over your creations.

paragraphs.name: fcc1
paragraphs.text: I try…

paragraphs.name: 3ce6
paragraphs.text: For pre-made laser cut projects, or laser cut inspo, check out Thingiverse.

paragraphs.name: de7d
paragraphs.text: Preparing Your Drawing for Printing

paragraphs.name: a764
paragraphs.text: If there are some lines you only want to lightly engrave, and others you want to intensely cut through, you can prepare your vector drawing for that by adjusting lines’ stroke and colour settings. These different settings can help you differentiate the lines when you open your your laser cutting software (I used RetinaEngrave).
I used thick blue lines (0.8 mm stroke width) for what I want to cut through, and black for what I want to engrave.

paragraphs.name: ed68
paragraphs.text: Start Cutting

paragraphs.name: e525
paragraphs.text: Yes, the loud sound is normal. No, your co-workers cannot hear you (?). But, knowing that you are making cool things can be motivation enough to disturb them anyway. Just kidding.

paragraphs.name: 2a64
paragraphs.text: Before cutting, you would need to ‘Home’ the laser. Ensure there is 2.0 cm distance between the laser and the material you are cutting. Ensure a fire extinguisher is nearby (no joke, not that you would likely use it).

paragraphs.name: 9fe2
paragraphs.text: Settings to use

paragraphs.name: 19c0
paragraphs.text: In general, choose ‘Vector Cut’ setting instead of ‘Raster Engrave’. When using Vector Cut, the laser will follow the path of your drawing. Retina Engrave may occasionally be preferable for engraving, but I personally use Vector Cut for everything.

paragraphs.name: b1a6
paragraphs.text: To cut through 3.0mm acrylic, I used 100% laser intensity at maximum speed, and cut the pattern 5–6 times. To engrave acrylic, any setting less intense than the above will work. You can decide how deeply you wish to engrave.

paragraphs.name: e184
paragraphs.text: OMG, There is a Fire!

paragraphs.name: 6f0d
paragraphs.text: Yes. After filming the mini-fire with your phone and getting too excited over the poor video quality, you might start worrying a bit.

paragraphs.name: b8b9
paragraphs.text: If you had ensured sufficient distance between the laser and the material (2.0 cm in my case), you would not usually damage the machine.

paragraphs.name: f6bb
paragraphs.text: If you want to avoid a fire, and also facilitate quicker cleaner cutting, it is advised to remove the sticky protective sheet on the acrylic before you begin. Typically, it is the sticky protective sheet that catches fire when you cut.

paragraphs.name: 40a0
paragraphs.text: After Cutting (IMPORTANT!)

paragraphs.name: a022
paragraphs.text: A typical rookie mistake is to remove your material before it is fully cut through (due to poor gauge of laser intensity). This is disastrous because it is almost impossible to re-position your material back into its original position for more cuts.

paragraphs.name: eb08
paragraphs.text: Now, you are left with a semi-cut acrylic which will be wasted. :(

paragraphs.name: 0bd4
paragraphs.text: Before removing your cut material, it is adviseable to gently knock on the material and inspect it to ensure it has been fully cut through. If you are unsure, it is always good to err on the side of caution and cut more times. A wasted piece of acrylic can feel very depressing (personal experience).

paragraphs.name: febf
paragraphs.text: Extra: Combining Laser Cut Things to Make a 3D Structure
For my first laser cutting project, I was making a laptop/keyboard/iPad holder. This was created by fixing many acrylic plates together to create a 3D structure.
These are the two base structures I cut (not to scale). Which are fitted together to make a 3D laptop/keyboard/iPad holder.

paragraphs.name: 62e4
paragraphs.text: Laptop/keyboard/iPad holder.

paragraphs.name: f9f4
paragraphs.text: When creating grooves for fitting parts together, I recommend using trapeziums rather than a uniform rectangle. This ensures better fit. You also have more lee-way for mistake, in case of cutting discrepancies.

paragraphs.name: c088
paragraphs.text: Trapezium groove to fit a 3.0mm thick part: The longer width at the top is larger (3.8mm), while the shorter at the bottom width is just right (3.2mm).

paragraphs.name: d3db
paragraphs.text: Extra: Building More Robust Structures

paragraphs.name: 4a72
paragraphs.text: The way you design your structure can also have a huge impact on how quickly you structures will break. In general, thin pieces of acrylic break off easily. In creating grooves or other designs, always design for wider slabs.

paragraphs.name: 4b69
paragraphs.text: Thin is bad.

paragraphs.name: 227b
paragraphs.text: Wide is good.

paragraphs.name: 3ff4
paragraphs.text: Cleaning Up…

paragraphs.name: a54e
paragraphs.text: Congratulations, you have made your first laser cut thing! Remember to vacuum any scrap bits or dust in the laser cutting machine. This is so that they would not accumulate into a big life-threatening fire next time.

paragraphs.name: 9b8f
paragraphs.text: Enjoy :)

paragraphs.name: a8c4
paragraphs.text: Editor’s Note: At time of writing, Hongyi is deciding where to go for her first year of undergraduate studies, and is interning with Hustle Fund, a VC and a friend of the company. She did a variety of software, hardware, and education-related projects for us, and was generally pretty awesome; feel free to email us for an effusively positive testimonial.
